## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\alpha>0$, let
$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_{\Pi}\subseteq L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb
C^{3})$ be the transverse space with $\varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]],
let $\Lambda>0$, let $g_{1},\dots,g_{J}\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) satisfy
$$\operatorname{supp}g_{j}\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\},\qquad \frac{g_{j}}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h ,$$
let $\eta_{0}\in\mathbb R$ and let $c_{1},\dots,c_{J}\in\mathbb C$ with
$$M:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_{j}g_{j}\in\mathfrak h,\qquad M\ne0 .$$
Fix $\Delta\in\mathbb R$ and define the finite Borel measure
$$\nu_{b}(B):=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\mathbf 1_{B}\bigl(\varepsilon(k)\bigr) \|M(k)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2}\,d^{3}k,\qquad K_{t}(x):=\frac{1}{\hbar^{2}t}\Bigl|\int_{0}^{t}e^{ixs/\hbar}\,ds\Bigr|^{2}\ \ (t>0),$$
and the vector-valued function
$$A_{b}(k,t):=-\frac{i\eta_{0}}{\hbar}M(k)\int_{0}^{t} e^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}\,ds\qquad(t\ge0).$$
Then:

(a) (factorisation) for every $t>0$ and almost every $k\in\mathbb R^{3}$,
$$|A_{b}(k,t)|^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}\,t\,K_{t}\bigl(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta\bigr) \|M(k)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2},$$
and consequently
$\|A_{b}(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}t\int_{\mathbb R}
K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)$;

(b) (normalisation) for every $t>0$ the denominator
$\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)$ is finite and strictly positive,
so
$$P_{t}(B):=\frac{\int_{B}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)} {\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)}$$
defines a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with
$P_{t}(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$;

(c) (concentration) if $\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ for some $J_{b}\in
L^{1}(\lambda)$ with $J_{b}=0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on
$\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda]$, if $J_{b}$ is continuous at some $\Delta$ with
$0<\Delta<\Lambda$ and $J_{b}(\Delta)>0$, and if $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is
continuous and bounded, then
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}f\,dP_{t}=f(\Delta);$$

(d) (positivity) if $\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ with $J_{b}\ge0$
$\lambda$-almost everywhere and $J_{b}>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on a
Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ of positive Lebesgue measure, then
$P_{t}(B)>0$ for every $t>0$;

(e) (tail concentration) under the hypotheses of (c), for every $\delta>0$,
$\lim_{t\to\infty}P_{t}\bigl(\{E:|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\}\bigr)=0$.

No dynamics, transition probability, rate, decay or physical identification is
asserted; the lemma computes an explicit kernel, its normalised push-forward
law and that law's limit.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the transverse space $\mathfrak h$, the cutoff data $\Lambda,g_{j}$, the coupling $\eta_{0}$, the coefficients $c_{j}$, the vector $M\ne0$, the number $\Delta$, the measure $\nu_{b}$, the kernel $K_{t}$ and the vectors $A_{b}(\cdot,t)$.

[F1] **Model objects.** $\mathfrak h=\{f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{3}):k\cdot f(k)=0\ \text{a.e.}\}$ is a closed subspace, $\varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|$ is continuous, $g_{j}\in\mathfrak h$ with $\operatorname{supp}g_{j}\subseteq\{0<\varepsilon\le\Lambda\}$ and $g_{j}/\sqrt\varepsilon\in\mathfrak h$, so $M\in\mathfrak h$ with $\operatorname{supp}M\subseteq\{0<\varepsilon\le\Lambda\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]], [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-cutoff-dipole-relative-bound]]).

[F2] **Kernel.** For $t>0$ and $x\ne0$, $K_{t}(x)=\dfrac{4\sin^{2}(xt/(2\hbar))}{x^{2}t}$ and $K_{t}(0)=t/\hbar^{2}$; $K_{t}\ge0$ is even and $\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(x)\,dx=2\pi/\hbar$; for $J\in L^{1}(\lambda)$ continuous at $\Delta$, $\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(x)J(\Delta+x)\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}J(\Delta)$ ([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-golden-rule-coefficient-approximate-identity]] clauses (a),(b)).

[F3] **The push-forward measure.** $\nu_{b}$ is a finite Borel measure with $\nu_{b}(\mathbb R)=\|M\|_{\mathfrak h}^{2}>0$, $\nu_{b}(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$, and $\int_{\mathbb R}f\,d\nu_{b}=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}f(\varepsilon(k))\|M(k)\|^{2}d^{3}k$ for every Borel $f\ge0$; for the vector $A_{b}$ of the statement, $\|A_{b}(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}t\int K_{t}(E-\Delta)d\nu_{b}(E)$ for $t>0$ and $A_{b}(\cdot,t)\in\mathfrak h$ ([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-golden-rule-coefficient-approximate-identity]] clauses (i),(ii)).

[F4] **Null sets of the kernel.** The set $\{x\in\mathbb R:K_{t}(x)=0\}$ equals $\{0\}\cup\{2\pi\hbar n/t:n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\}$, a countable hence Lebesgue-null subset of $\mathbb R$; in particular $K_{t}>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere and $K_{t}$ is bounded by $t/\hbar^{2}$ ([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-golden-rule-coefficient-approximate-identity]] clause (a), [[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]).

[F5] **Measure and integral calculus.** A measure with density $h$ is given by $(h\lambda)(B)=\int_{B}h\,d\lambda$; for a nonnegative measurable $f$ the map $B\mapsto\int_{B}f\,d\lambda$ is a measure, and $\int_{B}f\,d\lambda>0$ whenever $f\ge0$ almost everywhere, $f>0$ almost everywhere on a set $B$ of positive measure, and $f$ is measurable; translation $x\mapsto\Delta+x$ preserves $\lambda$ ([[def-measure-with-density]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

[F6] **Continuity and limits.** Continuity of $J_{b}$ at $\Delta$ and the meaning of $\lim_{t\to\infty}$ are those of [[def-continuity-real]] and [[def-limits-at-infinity]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; compute the squared modulus of the explicit amplitude, normalise the resulting measure using the strict positivity of the kernel off a null set, and apply the approximate identity of the cited golden-rule item to the density and to its tails.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F6].

1.1 [Factorisation] Let $t>0$. For every $k$ one has $\int_{0}^{t}e^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}ds\in\mathbb C$ and $|A_{b}(k,t)|^{2}=\frac{\eta_{0}^{2}}{\hbar^{2}}\|M(k)\|^{2}\bigl|\int_{0}^{t}e^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}ds\bigr|^{2}$; by the definition of $K_{t}$ with $x=\varepsilon(k)-\Delta$ the last factor equals $\hbar^{2}tK_{t}(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)$, giving the displayed pointwise identity. Integrating over $\mathbb R^{3}$ and using [F3] with $f=K_{t}(\cdot-\Delta)\ge0$ gives $\|A_{b}(\cdot,t)\|^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}t\int K_{t}(E-\Delta)d\nu_{b}(E)$. This is (a). [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 [Normalisation] By [F4], $K_{t}>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere and $K_{t}\le t/\hbar^{2}$; hence $K_{t}(\cdot-\Delta)>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere and $\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)d\nu_{b}(E)\le(t/\hbar^{2})\nu_{b}(\mathbb R)<\infty$. For strict positivity write the integral as $\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}K_{t}(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)\|M(k)\|^{2}d^{3}k$ by [F3]: the integrand is nonnegative, the set $\{k:M(k)\ne0\}$ has positive Lebesgue measure because $\|M\|_{\mathfrak h}^{2}=\int\|M(k)\|^{2}d^{3}k>0$ by $M\ne0$, and on that set $K_{t}(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)>0$ off a null set by [F4]; so the integral is strictly positive by [F5]. Therefore $P_{t}$ is a Borel probability measure, and $P_{t}(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$ because $\nu_{b}$ has that property and $K_{t}(\cdot-\Delta)$ is finite and positive off a null set. This is (b). [F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 [Concentration] Assume now $\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ with $J_{b}$ as in (c), and let $f$ be continuous and bounded, $|f|\le C$. For $t>0$, using [F5] to pass between $\nu_{b}$ and $\lambda$ and the translation $E=\Delta+x$, $$\int_{\mathbb R}f\,dP_{t}=\frac{\int_{\mathbb R}f(\Delta+x)K_{t}(x)J_{b}(\Delta+x)\,dx}{\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(x)J_{b}(\Delta+x)\,dx}.$$ The numerator is $\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(x)J(\Delta+x)dx$ with $J:=f\cdot J_{b}$, which lies in $L^{1}(\lambda)$ and is continuous at $\Delta$ because $f$ and $J_{b}$ are; the denominator is the same expression with $J:=J_{b}$. By [F2] the numerator tends to $\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}f(\Delta)J_{b}(\Delta)$ and the denominator to $\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}J_{b}(\Delta)$, which is strictly positive by hypothesis and step 1.2; hence the ratio tends to $f(\Delta)$. This is (c). [F2, F5, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 [Positivity on windows] Let $B$ be Borel with $\lambda(B)>0$ and $J_{b}>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on $B$. By [F5] and the density hypothesis, $P_{t}(B)=\bigl(\int_{B}K_{t}(E-\Delta)J_{b}(E)\,d\lambda(E)\bigr)\big/\bigl(\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)J_{b}(E)\,d\lambda(E)\bigr)$ with a finite positive denominator by step 1.2; the integrand of the numerator is nonnegative, and it is strictly positive almost everywhere on $B$ because $K_{t}(\cdot-\Delta)>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere by [F4] and $J_{b}>0$ almost everywhere on $B$; by [F5] the numerator is strictly positive, so $P_{t}(B)>0$. This is (d). [F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 [Tails] Under the hypotheses of (c), fix $\delta>0$ and let $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $\varphi(x):=\max\{0,\min\{1,2(|x|-\delta/2)/\delta\}\}$, which is continuous and bounded with $\varphi=0$ on $[-\delta/2,\delta/2]$ and $\varphi=1$ on $\{|x|\ge\delta\}$. Then $\mathbf 1_{\{|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\}}\le\varphi(E-\Delta)$ pointwise, so $P_{t}(\{|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\})\le\int\varphi\,dP_{t}$, and step 2.1 with $f:=\varphi$ gives $\lim_{t\to\infty}\int\varphi\,dP_{t}=\varphi(0)=0$; hence the tails tend to zero. This is (e). [step 2.1, F6, algebra]

4.1 [Assembly and scope] Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove (a) and (b); step 2.1 proves (c); step 2.2 proves (d); step 3.1 proves (e). Nothing in the argument used a dynamics, a transition probability, a rate, a measurement or a physical identification; the statement's scope paragraph records this. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **What concentrates.** Clause (c) says that the normalised energy law of the explicit single-vertex vector converges to the unit mass at the parameter $\Delta$ whenever the photon density has a continuous positive value there; clause (d) shows that at every finite time a window on which the density is positive almost everywhere still carries strictly positive probability. The two are compatible: the window probability tends to zero only for windows separated from $\Delta$, and the convergence is of the law, not of the density.
- **No physical spike.** The limit in (c) is a limit of an ideal model law as the parameter $t$ of the explicit vector grows; it is not an assertion that a physical line is sharp or that a measurement at time $t$ has a sharp outcome.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\hbar>0$, $\alpha>0$, the transverse space $\mathfrak h$, the cutoff data $\Lambda,g_{j}$, the coupling $\eta_{0}$, the coefficients $c_{j}$, the vector $M$ (nonzero only for the normalized-law claims), the number $\Delta$, the measure $\nu_{b}$, the kernel $K_{t}$ and the vectors $A_{b}(\cdot,t)$.

[F1] **Transverse space and the declared cutoff data.** The space $\mathfrak h=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):k\cdot f(k)=0\text{ a.e.}\}$ is a closed linear subspace and $\varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|$ is continuous ([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]] clause (a)). The vectors $g_j$, their common energy cutoff, the arbitrary complex coefficients $c_j$ and the finite sum $M=\sum_jc_jg_j$ are the given data; no dipole-matrix or atomic-eigenvector constraint on these coefficients is assumed.

[F2] **The unchanged scalar kernel supplier.** For $\hbar>0$, $t>0$ and $x\ne0$, $K_t(x)=4\sin^2(xt/(2\hbar))/(x^2t)$ and $K_t(0)=t/\hbar^2>0$. The kernel is continuous, nonnegative and even, has mass $2\pi/\hbar$, and for $J\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ continuous at $\Delta$ one has $\int K_t(x)J(\Delta+x)\,dx\to(2\pi/\hbar)J(\Delta)$ ([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-golden-rule-coefficient-approximate-identity]] clauses (a),(b)). Only these scalar clauses are used; its more restricted emission-coefficient clause (c) is not applied to the present arbitrary coefficients.

[F3] **Definition of the push-forward.** The set function is $\nu_b(B)=\int\mathbf1_B(\varepsilon(k))\|M(k)\|^2d^3k$. Its measure property, total mass, support and nonnegative integration identity for the present arbitrary $M$ are proved in step 1.1 directly from this definition.

[F4] **Null-set suppliers.** A countable subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is Lebesgue null under CC ([[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). For every nonnegative Borel $g$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $\int g(k)d^3k=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^2}g(r\omega)r^2d\sigma(\omega)dr$, with finite sphere measure $\sigma$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], Statement with $n=3$). These will prove nullity of the actual energy-level spheres, rather than inferring a null pullback from one-dimensional nullity alone.

[F5] **Measure and integration.** A measure with density $h$ satisfies $(h\lambda)(B)=\int_Bh\,d\lambda$. Nonnegative integrals and finite sums are additive, increasing nonnegative simple functions approximate nonnegative Borel functions, and monotone convergence applies ([[def-measure-with-density]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). Translation $E=\Delta+x$ preserves Lebesgue integrals of integrable functions ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]). A nonnegative measurable function positive on a positive-measure set has positive integral: if its integral were zero, each set on which it is at least $1/n$ would be null, so their countable union could not have positive measure.

[F6] **Continuity and limits.** The declared continuity and limit conventions are those of [[def-continuity-real]] and [[def-limits-at-infinity]]. For a complex integrable function, its integral and limits can be computed by its real and imaginary parts.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; prove the push-forward for arbitrary coefficients, compute the amplitude, verify nullity of the actual momentum spheres, normalize, and apply the unchanged scalar approximate identity with correctly shifted test functions.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]–[F6], in particular $\hbar>0$; only the normalized-law claims assume $M\ne0$.



1.1 [Arbitrary-coefficient push-forward] Since $\mathfrak h$ is linear, the finite sum $M$ lies in it, with $\|M\|_2\le\sum_j|c_j|\|g_j\|_2<\infty$. The common cutoff gives $M=0$ a.e. outside $\{0<\varepsilon\le\Lambda\}$. The weight $\|M\|^2$ is nonnegative and integrable, and the inverse image of a Borel set under continuous $\varepsilon$ is Borel. Thus $\nu_b$ is nonnegative and finite, with $\nu_b(\mathbb R)=\|M\|_2^2$ and the stated support. For disjoint Borel $B_i$, the inverse-image indicators of their finite unions increase to the indicator of their union; monotone convergence gives countable additivity. The identity $\int f\,d\nu_b=\int f(\varepsilon(k))\|M(k)\|^2d^3k$ holds first for indicators by definition, then for nonnegative simple functions by finite additivity and then for every nonnegative Borel $f$ by monotone convergence. It also holds for integrable real or complex functions by their positive/negative or real/imaginary decompositions. All conclusions include $M=0$ and do not import the source's special matrix coefficients. [given, F1, F5, algebra]

1.2 [Exact zeros and their momentum pullback] Since $K_t(0)=t/\hbar^2>0$, its zero set is exactly $Z_t=\{2\pi\hbar n/t:n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\}$ by [F2], and this is countable and one-dimensionally null by [F4]. The zeros of $K_t(E-\Delta)$ form $\Delta+Z_t$. For each fixed energy $E$, $\varepsilon^{-1}(\{E\})$ is empty if $E<0$, is the singleton $\{0\}$ if $E=0$, and is the sphere $\{|k|=E/\alpha\}$ if $E>0$. The singleton is null by [F4]. For a positive radius $r_0$, apply the polar formula [F4] to the indicator of $\{|k|=r_0\}$: its integral is $\sigma(S^2)\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{r_0\}}(r)r^2dr=0$ because the one-dimensional singleton is null. Thus every such energy level is null in $\mathbb R^3$, and the countable union $\varepsilon^{-1}(\Delta+Z_t)$ is null by countable subadditivity. Consequently $K_t(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)>0$ for a.e. momentum $k$. This establishes the exact needed pullback statement for arbitrary real $\Delta$. [given, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 [Amplitude and factorization including zero cases] For $t\ge0$ the time integral $I_t(E)=\int_0^te^{i(E-\Delta)s/\hbar}ds$ is continuous in $E$ and bounded by $t$. Therefore $A_b(k,t)=-(i\eta_0/\hbar)I_t(\varepsilon(k))M(k)$ is an $L^2$ vector with norm at most $|\eta_0|t\|M\|_2/\hbar$, and scalar multiplication preserves transversality, so $A_b(\cdot,t)\in\mathfrak h$. At $t=0$ it is zero. For $t>0$, the kernel definition gives $|I_t(E)|^2=\hbar^2tK_t(E-\Delta)$; hence $\|A_b(k,t)\|^2=\eta_0^2tK_t(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)\|M(k)\|^2$ a.e. Integrating with step 1.1 proves the norm formula in (a). If $M=0$ or $\eta_0=0$, both sides are zero; no division by that norm was used. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F5, algebra]

3.1 [Normalization when M is nonzero] The defining time integral has modulus at most $t$, so $0\le K_t(x)\le t/\hbar^2$ everywhere. Thus $d_t:=\int K_t(E-\Delta)d\nu_b(E)\le(t/\hbar^2)\|M\|_2^2<\infty$. If $M\ne0$, the set on which $\|M(k)\|^2>0$ has positive Lebesgue measure. By step 1.2, the product $K_t(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)\|M(k)\|^2$ is positive a.e. on that set, and its integral is positive by [F5]. Step 1.1 makes this integral exactly $d_t$. Hence $B\mapsto d_t^{-1}\int_BK_t(E-\Delta)d\nu_b(E)$ is a Borel probability measure, and its support is in $(0,\Lambda]$ because $\nu_b$ has that support. This proves (b). For $\eta_0=0$, $A_b=0$ but this formal normalized kernel law is still defined whenever $M\ne0$; it is not asserted to arise by normalizing the zero amplitude. If $M=0$ then $d_t=0$ and no normalized law is asserted. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, F2, F5, algebra]

4.1 [Concentration for every bounded continuous complex test] Assume (c), and let $f$ be bounded continuous. The density equality and translation from [F5] give $\int f\,dP_t=\bigl(\int K_t(x)f(\Delta+x)J_b(\Delta+x)dx\bigr)/\bigl(\int K_t(x)J_b(\Delta+x)dx\bigr)$; both integrals are finite because $K_t$ is bounded and $J_b,fJ_b\in L^1$. The function $fJ_b$ is continuous at $\Delta$, so [F2] applied to its real and imaginary parts makes the numerator tend to $(2\pi/\hbar)f(\Delta)J_b(\Delta)$. Applied to $J_b$ it makes the denominator tend to $(2\pi/\hbar)J_b(\Delta)>0$. The denominator is also strictly positive at every time by step 3.1. The ratio therefore tends to $f(\Delta)$, proving (c), with no restriction that the test or coefficients be real. [step 3.1, F2, F5, F6, algebra]

4.2 [Positive-measure windows] Under (d), the numerator $\int_BK_t(E-\Delta)J_b(E)dE$ is nonnegative and is strictly positive a.e. on the positive-measure Borel set $B$: $J_b>0$ a.e. there, and the kernel vanishes only on the countable energy set $\Delta+Z_t$ from step 1.2. By [F5] its integral is positive, whereas step 3.1 gives a finite positive denominator. Thus $P_t(B)>0$ for every $t>0$, proving (d). [step 1.2, step 3.1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

5.1 [Correctly shifted tail test] Under (c), fix $\delta>0$ and put $\varphi_\delta(x)=\max\{0,\min\{1,2(|x|-\delta/2)/\delta\}\}$. This is continuous, lies between zero and one, vanishes on $|x|\le\delta/2$, and equals one on $|x|\ge\delta$. Use the bounded continuous function $f_\delta(E)=\varphi_\delta(E-\Delta)$, so $f_\delta(\Delta)=\varphi_\delta(0)=0$. Pointwise $\mathbf1_{\{|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\}}\le f_\delta(E)$, whence $0\le P_t(\{|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\})\le\int f_\delta\,dP_t\to f_\delta(\Delta)=0$ by step 4.1. This proves (e) with the required energy shift. [step 4.1, F6, algebra]

6.1 [Assembly and scope] Step 2.1 proves (a) including every zero case; step 3.1 proves (b) only for $M\ne0$; steps 4.1–5.1 give the full concentration, positivity and tail claims. The arbitrary-vector push-forward was established locally in step 1.1, and the scalar kernel/approximate-identity clauses of the source were used unchanged. No dynamics, physical transition probability, rate, detector identification or normalization of a zero physical amplitude was asserted. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **What concentrates.** Clause (c) says that the normalised energy law of the explicit single-vertex vector converges to the unit mass at the parameter $\Delta$ whenever the photon density has a continuous positive value there; clause (d) shows that at every finite time a window on which the density is positive almost everywhere still carries strictly positive probability. The two are compatible: the window probability tends to zero only for windows separated from $\Delta$, and the convergence is of the law, not of the density.
- **No physical spike.** The limit in (c) is a limit of an ideal model law as the parameter $t$ of the explicit vector grows; it is not an assertion that a physical line is sharp or that a measurement at time $t$ has a sharp outcome.

- **Zero coupling and zero vector.** When $\eta_0=0$, the explicit amplitude vanishes, but the formal kernel law $P_t$ remains well-defined for $M\ne0$. When $M=0$, only the unnormalized factorization is asserted and all amplitudes vanish; no division by $\|A_b\|$ or zero denominator is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Axiom of Dependent Choice and the
Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the transverse
subspace
$$\mathfrak h:=\Bigl\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):\ k\cdot f(k)=0\ \text{for a.e. }k\Bigr\}$$
with the $L^2$ inner product, define the bounded multiplier-valued function
$\Pi(k):=\mathrm{id}-|k|^{-2}kk^{\mathsf T}$ for $k\ne0$ and $\Pi(0):=0$, and let
$M_\Pi$ be multiplication by $\Pi$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Write
$\varepsilon(k):=\alpha|k|$ and let $M_\varepsilon$ be multiplication by
$\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}:=M_\varepsilon|_{\mathfrak h}$.
Let $F(\mathfrak h)$ be the Fock space of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] with sectors
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and for $n\ge1$ define
$$T_n\psi:=\varepsilon_n\psi,\quad \varepsilon_n(k_1,\dots,k_n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha|k_i|,\qquad D(T_n):=\{\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}:\varepsilon_n\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\},$$
and $T_0:=0$ on $\mathbb C$. Finally put
$$H_f:=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T_n,\qquad D(H_f):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(\mathfrak h):\ \sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$
Then:

(a) $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ is a closed separable subspace of
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, invariant under $M_\varepsilon$, and
$\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on
$\mathfrak h$ with $D(\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h})=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\varepsilon f\in\mathfrak h\}$
([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]],
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]);

(b) each $T_n$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with the displayed domain
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]],
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]);

(c) $H_f$ is self-adjoint and positive with domain $D(H_f)$; it commutes with
every sector projection $\Pi_n$ (i.e. $T_n$ maps its sector into itself);

(d) for every $\beta>0$ the bounded operator $e^{-\beta H_f}$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]) is not compact and in particular not trace
class ([[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]); more
precisely its restriction to the one-particle sector equals the multiplication
operator $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ on $\mathfrak h$, which is not compact, and
the restriction of a compact operator to a closed invariant subspace is compact.

The identification of $\mathfrak h$, $\varepsilon$ and $H_f$ with physical
transverse photons in a chosen frame is a separate model assumption and is not
asserted here; no thermal interpretation of $e^{-\beta H_f}$ is claimed either.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\alpha>0$, let
$\mathfrak h$ be the transverse space and $H_f=\bigoplus_nT_n$ the free
transverse Fock Hamiltonian of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]],
and let $A_\pm(g)$, $g\in\mathfrak h$, be the maximal creation and annihilation
operators on $F(\mathfrak h)$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]]. Fix a cutoff
$\Lambda>0$ and vectors $g_1,\dots,g_J\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) with
$$\operatorname{supp}g_j\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\}\quad\text{and}\quad \frac{g_j}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h,\qquad \varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|,$$
and define the symmetric operator
$$\phi(g):=A_-(g)+A_+(g),\qquad D(\phi(g)):=D(H_f).$$
Let $d\ge1$, let $H_a$ be a Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix, and let
$D_1,\dots,D_J$ be Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices with operator norms
$\|D_j\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). Then:

(a) for every $\Psi\in D(H_f)$,
$$\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2\le\Bigl\|\frac g{\sqrt\varepsilon}\Bigr\|^2\langle H_f\Psi,\Psi\rangle,\qquad
\|A_+(g)\Psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\Psi\|^2;$$
in particular $\Psi\in D(A_+(g))\cap D(A_-(g))$ and for every $\eta>0$ there is
a finite $C_\eta$ with
$$\|\phi(g)\Psi\|\le\eta\|H_f\Psi\|+C_\eta\|\Psi\| ;$$

(b) $\phi(g)$ is symmetric on $D(H_f)$ and has $H_f$-bound zero
([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(c) the free part $H_0:=H_a\otimes I+I\otimes H_f$ with domain
$C^d\otimes D(H_f)$ is self-adjoint on $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)$
([[def-hilbert-space]]); for every $\eta_0\in\mathbb R$ the operator
$$H:=H_0+\eta_0\sum_{j=1}^JD_j\otimes\phi(g_j),\qquad D(H):=C^d\otimes D(H_f),$$
is self-adjoint on $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)$ and bounded below
([[thm-kato-rellich]],
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-bounded-fixed-n-operator]] (c)).

The product $D_j\otimes\phi(g_j)$ and the coupling $\eta_0$ carry the dimension
of energy in a physical normalisation; this normalisation is a model choice and
no physical statement about radiation or spontaneous emission is made here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\hbar>0$.

**(a) The golden-rule kernel.** For $t>0$ define
$$K_t(x):=\frac1{\hbar^2t}\Bigl|\int_0^te^{ixs/\hbar}\,ds\Bigr|^2,\qquad x\in\mathbb R .$$
Then $K_t$ is continuous, nonnegative and even, and for $x\ne0$
$$K_t(x)=\frac{4\sin^2\bigl(xt/(2\hbar)\bigr)}{x^2t},\qquad K_t(0)=\frac t{\hbar^2};$$
moreover for every $\delta>0$ and every $x$ with $|x|\ge\delta$,
$$K_t(x)\le\frac4{x^2t}\le\frac4{\delta^2t},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}K_t(x)\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}.$$

**(b) Approximate identity.** Let $J\in L^1(\mathbb R)$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]) and let $\Delta\in\mathbb R$.
If the representative $J$ is continuous at $\Delta$
([[def-continuity-real]]), then
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}K_t(x)J(\Delta+x)\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}J(\Delta)$$
([[def-limits-at-infinity]]).

**(c) First-order emission coefficient.** Adopt the objects and hypotheses of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-cutoff-dipole-relative-bound]]: $\alpha>0$, the
transverse space $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]]
with $\varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|$, the cutoff $\Lambda>0$, the vectors
$g_1,\dots,g_J\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) with
$$\operatorname{supp}g_j\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\},\qquad \frac{g_j}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h,$$
the Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices $H_a,D_1,\dots,D_J$ and the coupling
$\eta_0\in\mathbb R$. Let $v_a,v_b$ be orthonormal eigenvectors of $H_a$ with
$H_av_a=E_av_a$, $H_av_b=E_av_b$, and let $\Delta:=E_a-E_b>0$. Put
$$c_j:=\langle D_jv_a,v_b\rangle\ (\mathbb C^d\text{ inner product}),\qquad M:=\sum_{j=1}^Jc_jg_j\in\mathfrak h,$$
and define the finite Borel measure
$$\nu_b(A):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf 1_A(\varepsilon(k))\,\|M(k)\|^2\,d^3k, \qquad A\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel},$$
and for $t\ge0$ the amplitude
$$A_b(k,t):=-\frac{i\eta_0}{\hbar}M(k)\int_0^te^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}\,ds .$$
Then:

(i) $\nu_b$ is a finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R$ with
$\nu_b(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$, and
$$\int_{\mathbb R}f\,d\nu_b=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(\varepsilon(k))\,\|M(k)\|^2\,d^3k$$
for every Borel $f\ge0$;

(ii) $A_b(\cdot,t)\in\mathfrak h$ for every $t\ge0$, and
for $t>0$,
$$\|A_b(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^2 =\eta_0^2t\int_{\mathbb R}K_t(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_b(E).$$
At $t=0$ the amplitude is zero, so its squared norm is zero; no $K_0$ is used.

(iii) if $\nu_b=J_b\lambda$ for some $J_b\in L^1(\lambda)$ with $J_b=0$
$\lambda$-a.e. on $\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda]$ and the representative $J_b$
continuous at $\Delta$, then for $0<\Delta<\Lambda$
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t\|A_b(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^2 =\frac{2\pi\eta_0^2}{\hbar}J_b(\Delta);$$
if instead $\Delta>\Lambda$, then the same limit exists and equals $0$. The
boundary case $\Delta=\Lambda$ is not asserted.

*Motivation and scope.* In the cutoff dipole model of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-cutoff-dipole-relative-bound]] the vector
$A_b(\cdot,t)$ is the explicit single-vertex amplitude with the atom passing
from $v_a$ to $v_b$ and one photon emitted; $\|A_b(\cdot,t)\|^2$ is the
corresponding first-order photon coefficient, and (iii) is the golden-rule
limit of that coefficient divided by $t$. This item computes only the limit of
the explicit coefficient, under the stated hypotheses on the spectral density
$J_b$. It asserts no approximation of the exact model evolution, no all-time or
weak-coupling limit, no Markov property and no exact exponential decay, and it
reports no measurement or empirical rate. The parameter $\hbar$, the coupling
$\eta_0$ and the matrices $D_j$ enter as mathematical normalisation data of the
model; their physical identification is a separate assumption.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Throughout, $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are **abbreviations and not real numbers**,
exactly as in [[def-interval]] and [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]. Every phrase
below is a single abbreviation for a displayed condition on reals, and no
arithmetic is ever performed with the symbols.

**Limits at $+\infty$.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be **not bounded above**
([[def-bounded-set]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. We
write

$$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$$

when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $M$ such that

$$|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for every } x \in A \text{ with } x > M .$$

**Limits at $-\infty$.** Let $A$ be **not bounded below**. We write
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L$ when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a
real $M$ with $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in A$ with $x < M$.

**Why unboundedness is required.** It plays exactly the role the limit-point
condition plays in [[def-function-limit]]. Saying that $A$ is not bounded above
says that no real is an upper bound of $A$, that is, that for every real $M$
there is $x \in A$ with $x > M$ ([[def-bounded-set]],
[[def-complete-ordered-field]]); so the set over which the condition quantifies
is never empty and the condition is never vacuous. Without the hypothesis every
real $L$ would satisfy it and the notation would not denote.

**Uniqueness, proved here.** Suppose $A$ is not bounded above and
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L'$ with
$L \ne L'$. Then $|L - L'| > 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), so
$\varepsilon := |L - L'|/2 > 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]],
[[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]). Choose reals $M_1, M_2$
witnessing the two conditions at this $\varepsilon$ and let $M$ be the larger of
them, the order being total. Since $A$ is not bounded above there is $x \in A$
with $x > M$, hence with $x > M_1$ and $x > M_2$, and then

$$|L - L'| = |(L - f(x)) + (f(x) - L')| \le |f(x) - L| + |f(x) - L'| < 2\varepsilon = |L - L'|$$

([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-add-order]]),
which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$, and the notation
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x)$ denotes a single real. The same four lines, with the
inequalities on $x$ reversed, give uniqueness at $-\infty$.

**Infinite limits at a point.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We write

$$f(x) \to +\infty \ \text{ as } \ x \to c$$

when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $f(x) > M$ for
every $x \in A$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$; and $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to c$
when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $f(x) < M$ for every
such $x$.

**This library does not write $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = +\infty$.** The right-hand
side would not be an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and writing the equation would
silently move the discussion into the extended real line, a structure that is
not a field. That is the convention already fixed by
[[def-divergence-to-infinity]] for sequences and by [[rem-sup-conventions]] for
suprema, and it is kept here. In particular none of the rules of
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]] may be applied to a function tending to
$\pm\infty$.

**Combined forms.** Let $A$ be not bounded above and $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We
write $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to +\infty$ when for every real $N$ there is a
real $M$ with $f(x) > N$ for every $x \in A$ with $x > M$. The other forms are
obtained the same way, by pairing one of the two conditions on $x$ (unbounded
above, unbounded below) with one of the two conditions on $f(x)$ (above every
real, below every real); each is again a single abbreviation for the displayed
condition, and none of them is an equation.

derivations.claim: [Factorisation] Let $t>0$. For every $k$ one has $\int_{0}^{t}e^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}ds\in\mathbb C$ and $|A_{b}(k,t)|^{2}=\frac{\eta_{0}^{2}}{\hbar^{2}}\|M(k)\|^{2}\bigl|\int_{0}^{t}e^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}ds\bigr|^{2}$; by the definition of $K_{t}$ with $x=\varepsilon(k)-\Delta$ the last factor equals $\hbar^{2}tK_{t}(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)$, giving the displayed pointwise identity. Integrating over $\mathbb R^{3}$ and using [F3] with $f=K_{t}(\cdot-\Delta)\ge0$ gives $\|A_{b}(\cdot,t)\|^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}t\int K_{t}(E-\Delta)d\nu_{b}(E)$. This is (a). [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

[Normalisation] By [F4], $K_{t}>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere and $K_{t}\le t/\hbar^{2}$; hence $K_{t}(\cdot-\Delta)>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere and $\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)d
u_{b}(E)\le(t/\hbar^{2})
u_{b}(\mathbb R)<\infty$. For strict positivity write the integral as $\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}K_{t}(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)\|M(k)\|^{2}d^{3}k$ by [F3]: the integrand is nonnegative, the set $\{k:M(k)
e0\}$ has positive Lebesgue measure because $\|M\|_{\mathfrak h}^{2}=\int\|M(k)\|^{2}d^{3}k>0$ by $M
e0$, and on that set $K_{t}(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)>0$ off a null set by [F4]; so the integral is strictly positive by [F5]. Therefore $P_{t}$ is a Borel probability measure, and $P_{t}(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$ because $
u_{b}$ has that property and $K_{t}(\cdot-\Delta)$ is finite and positive off a null set. This is (b). [F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

[Concentration] Assume now $\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ with $J_{b}$ as in (c), and let $f$ be continuous and bounded, $|f|\le C$. For $t>0$, using [F5] to pass between $\nu_{b}$ and $\lambda$ and the translation $E=\Delta+x$, $$\int_{\mathbb R}f\,dP_{t}=\frac{\int_{\mathbb R}f(\Delta+x)K_{t}(x)J_{b}(\Delta+x)\,dx}{\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(x)J_{b}(\Delta+x)\,dx}.$$ The numerator is $\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(x)J(\Delta+x)dx$ with $J:=f\cdot J_{b}$, which lies in $L^{1}(\lambda)$ and is continuous at $\Delta$ because $f$ and $J_{b}$ are; the denominator is the same expression with $J:=J_{b}$. By [F2] the numerator tends to $\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}f(\Delta)J_{b}(\Delta)$ and the denominator to $\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}J_{b}(\Delta)$, which is strictly positive by hypothesis and step 1.2; hence the ratio tends to $f(\Delta)$. This is (c). [F2, F5, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

[Positivity on windows] Let $B$ be Borel with $\lambda(B)>0$ and $J_{b}>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on $B$. By [F5] and the density hypothesis, $P_{t}(B)=\bigl(\int_{B}K_{t}(E-\Delta)J_{b}(E)\,d\lambda(E)\bigr)\big/\bigl(\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)J_{b}(E)\,d\lambda(E)\bigr)$ with a finite positive denominator by step 1.2; the integrand of the numerator is nonnegative, and it is strictly positive almost everywhere on $B$ because $K_{t}(\cdot-\Delta)>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere by [F4] and $J_{b}>0$ almost everywhere on $B$; by [F5] the numerator is strictly positive, so $P_{t}(B)>0$. This is (d). [F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

[Tails] Under the hypotheses of (c), fix $\delta>0$ and let $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $\varphi(x):=\max\{0,\min\{1,2(|x|-\delta/2)/\delta\}\}$, which is continuous and bounded with $\varphi=0$ on $[-\delta/2,\delta/2]$ and $\varphi=1$ on $\{|x|\ge\delta\}$. Then $\mathbf 1_{\{|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\}}\le\varphi(E-\Delta)$ pointwise, so $P_{t}(\{|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\})\le\int\varphi\,dP_{t}$, and step 2.1 with $f:=\varphi$ gives $\lim_{t\to\infty}\int\varphi\,dP_{t}=\varphi(0)=0$; hence the tails tend to zero. This is (e). [step 2.1, F6, algebra]

[Assembly and scope] Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove (a) and (b); step 2.1 proves (c); step 2.2 proves (d); step 3.1 proves (e). Nothing in the argument used a dynamics, a transition probability, a rate, a measurement or a physical identification; the statement's scope paragraph records this. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

before.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Axiom of Dependent Choice and the
Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the transverse
subspace
$$\mathfrak h:=\Bigl\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):\ k\cdot f(k)=0\ \text{for a.e. }k\Bigr\}$$
with the $L^2$ inner product, define the bounded multiplier-valued function
$\Pi(k):=\mathrm{id}-|k|^{-2}kk^{\mathsf T}$ for $k\ne0$ and $\Pi(0):=0$, and let
$M_\Pi$ be multiplication by $\Pi$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Write
$\varepsilon(k):=\alpha|k|$ and let $M_\varepsilon$ be multiplication by
$\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}:=M_\varepsilon|_{\mathfrak h}$.
Let $F(\mathfrak h)$ be the Fock space of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] with sectors
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and for $n\ge1$ define
$$T_n\psi:=\varepsilon_n\psi,\quad \varepsilon_n(k_1,\dots,k_n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha|k_i|,\qquad D(T_n):=\{\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}:\varepsilon_n\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\},$$
and $T_0:=0$ on $\mathbb C$. Finally put
$$H_f:=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T_n,\qquad D(H_f):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(\mathfrak h):\ \sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$
Then:

(a) $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ is a closed separable subspace of
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, invariant under $M_\varepsilon$, and
$\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on
$\mathfrak h$ with $D(\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h})=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\varepsilon f\in\mathfrak h\}$
([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]],
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]);

(b) each $T_n$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with the displayed domain
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]],
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]);

(c) $H_f$ is self-adjoint and positive with domain $D(H_f)$; it commutes with
every sector projection $\Pi_n$ (i.e. $T_n$ maps its sector into itself);

(d) for every $\beta>0$ the bounded operator $e^{-\beta H_f}$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]) is not compact and in particular not trace
class ([[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]); more
precisely its restriction to the one-particle sector equals the multiplication
operator $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ on $\mathfrak h$, which is not compact, and
the restriction of a compact operator to a closed invariant subspace is compact.

The identification of $\mathfrak h$, $\varepsilon$ and $H_f$ with physical
transverse photons in a chosen frame is a separate model assumption and is not
asserted here; no thermal interpretation of $e^{-\beta H_f}$ is claimed either.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\alpha>0$, let
$\mathfrak h$ be the transverse space and $H_f=\bigoplus_nT_n$ the free
transverse Fock Hamiltonian of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]],
and let $A_\pm(g)$, $g\in\mathfrak h$, be the maximal creation and annihilation
operators on $F(\mathfrak h)$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]]. Fix a cutoff
$\Lambda>0$ and vectors $g_1,\dots,g_J\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) with
$$\operatorname{supp}g_j\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\}\quad\text{and}\quad \frac{g_j}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h,\qquad \varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|,$$
and define the symmetric operator
$$\phi(g):=A_-(g)+A_+(g),\qquad D(\phi(g)):=D(H_f).$$
Let $d\ge1$, let $H_a$ be a Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix, and let
$D_1,\dots,D_J$ be Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices with operator norms
$\|D_j\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). Then:

(a) for every $\Psi\in D(H_f)$,
$$\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2\le\Bigl\|\frac g{\sqrt\varepsilon}\Bigr\|^2\langle H_f\Psi,\Psi\rangle,\qquad
\|A_+(g)\Psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\Psi\|^2;$$
in particular $\Psi\in D(A_+(g))\cap D(A_-(g))$ and for every $\eta>0$ there is
a finite $C_\eta$ with
$$\|\phi(g)\Psi\|\le\eta\|H_f\Psi\|+C_\eta\|\Psi\| ;$$

(b) $\phi(g)$ is symmetric on $D(H_f)$ and has $H_f$-bound zero
([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(c) the free part $H_0:=H_a\otimes I+I\otimes H_f$ with domain
$C^d\otimes D(H_f)$ is self-adjoint on $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)$
([[def-hilbert-space]]); for every $\eta_0\in\mathbb R$ the operator
$$H:=H_0+\eta_0\sum_{j=1}^JD_j\otimes\phi(g_j),\qquad D(H):=C^d\otimes D(H_f),$$
is self-adjoint on $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)$ and bounded below
([[thm-kato-rellich]],
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-bounded-fixed-n-operator]] (c)).

The product $D_j\otimes\phi(g_j)$ and the coupling $\eta_0$ carry the dimension
of energy in a physical normalisation; this normalisation is a model choice and
no physical statement about radiation or spontaneous emission is made here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\hbar>0$.

**(a) The golden-rule kernel.** For $t>0$ define
$$K_t(x):=\frac1{\hbar^2t}\Bigl|\int_0^te^{ixs/\hbar}\,ds\Bigr|^2,\qquad x\in\mathbb R .$$
Then $K_t$ is continuous, nonnegative and even, and for $x\ne0$
$$K_t(x)=\frac{4\sin^2\bigl(xt/(2\hbar)\bigr)}{x^2t},\qquad K_t(0)=\frac t{\hbar^2};$$
moreover for every $\delta>0$ and every $x$ with $|x|\ge\delta$,
$$K_t(x)\le\frac4{x^2t}\le\frac4{\delta^2t},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}K_t(x)\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}.$$

**(b) Approximate identity.** Let $J\in L^1(\mathbb R)$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]) and let $\Delta\in\mathbb R$.
If the representative $J$ is continuous at $\Delta$
([[def-continuity-real]]), then
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}K_t(x)J(\Delta+x)\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}J(\Delta)$$
([[def-limits-at-infinity]]).

**(c) First-order emission coefficient.** Adopt the objects and hypotheses of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-cutoff-dipole-relative-bound]]: $\alpha>0$, the
transverse space $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]]
with $\varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|$, the cutoff $\Lambda>0$, the vectors
$g_1,\dots,g_J\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) with
$$\operatorname{supp}g_j\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\},\qquad \frac{g_j}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h,$$
the Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices $H_a,D_1,\dots,D_J$ and the coupling
$\eta_0\in\mathbb R$. Let $v_a,v_b$ be orthonormal eigenvectors of $H_a$ with
$H_av_a=E_av_a$, $H_av_b=E_av_b$, and let $\Delta:=E_a-E_b>0$. Put
$$c_j:=\langle D_jv_a,v_b\rangle\ (\mathbb C^d\text{ inner product}),\qquad M:=\sum_{j=1}^Jc_jg_j\in\mathfrak h,$$
and define the finite Borel measure
$$\nu_b(A):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf 1_A(\varepsilon(k))\,\|M(k)\|^2\,d^3k, \qquad A\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel},$$
and for $t\ge0$ the amplitude
$$A_b(k,t):=-\frac{i\eta_0}{\hbar}M(k)\int_0^te^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}\,ds .$$
Then:

(i) $\nu_b$ is a finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R$ with
$\nu_b(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$, and
$$\int_{\mathbb R}f\,d\nu_b=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(\varepsilon(k))\,\|M(k)\|^2\,d^3k$$
for every Borel $f\ge0$;

(ii) $A_b(\cdot,t)\in\mathfrak h$ for every $t\ge0$, and
for $t>0$,
$$\|A_b(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^2 =\eta_0^2t\int_{\mathbb R}K_t(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_b(E).$$
At $t=0$ the amplitude is zero, so its squared norm is zero; no $K_0$ is used.

(iii) if $\nu_b=J_b\lambda$ for some $J_b\in L^1(\lambda)$ with $J_b=0$
$\lambda$-a.e. on $\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda]$ and the representative $J_b$
continuous at $\Delta$, then for $0<\Delta<\Lambda$
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t\|A_b(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^2 =\frac{2\pi\eta_0^2}{\hbar}J_b(\Delta);$$
if instead $\Delta>\Lambda$, then the same limit exists and equals $0$. The
boundary case $\Delta=\Lambda$ is not asserted.

*Motivation and scope.* In the cutoff dipole model of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-cutoff-dipole-relative-bound]] the vector
$A_b(\cdot,t)$ is the explicit single-vertex amplitude with the atom passing
from $v_a$ to $v_b$ and one photon emitted; $\|A_b(\cdot,t)\|^2$ is the
corresponding first-order photon coefficient, and (iii) is the golden-rule
limit of that coefficient divided by $t$. This item computes only the limit of
the explicit coefficient, under the stated hypotheses on the spectral density
$J_b$. It asserts no approximation of the exact model evolution, no all-time or
weak-coupling limit, no Markov property and no exact exponential decay, and it
reports no measurement or empirical rate. The parameter $\hbar$, the coupling
$\eta_0$ and the matrices $D_j$ enter as mathematical normalisation data of the
model; their physical identification is a separate assumption.

and for $t\ge0$ the amplitude
$$A_b(k,t):=-\frac{i\eta_0}{\hbar}M(k)\int_0^te^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}\,ds .$$
Then:

(i) $\nu_b$ is a finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R$ with
$\nu_b(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$, and
$$\int_{\mathbb R}f\,d\nu_b=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(\varepsilon(k))\,\|M(k)\|^2\,d^3k$$
for every Borel $f\ge0$;

(ii) $A_b(\cdot,t)\in\mathfrak h$ for every $t\ge0$, and
for $t>0$,

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Throughout, $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are **abbreviations and not real numbers**,
exactly as in [[def-interval]] and [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]. Every phrase
below is a single abbreviation for a displayed condition on reals, and no
arithmetic is ever performed with the symbols.

**Limits at $+\infty$.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be **not bounded above**
([[def-bounded-set]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. We
write

$$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$$

when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $M$ such that

$$|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for every } x \in A \text{ with } x > M .$$

**Limits at $-\infty$.** Let $A$ be **not bounded below**. We write
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L$ when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a
real $M$ with $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in A$ with $x < M$.

**Why unboundedness is required.** It plays exactly the role the limit-point
condition plays in [[def-function-limit]]. Saying that $A$ is not bounded above
says that no real is an upper bound of $A$, that is, that for every real $M$
there is $x \in A$ with $x > M$ ([[def-bounded-set]],
[[def-complete-ordered-field]]); so the set over which the condition quantifies
is never empty and the condition is never vacuous. Without the hypothesis every
real $L$ would satisfy it and the notation would not denote.

**Uniqueness, proved here.** Suppose $A$ is not bounded above and
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L'$ with
$L \ne L'$. Then $|L - L'| > 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), so
$\varepsilon := |L - L'|/2 > 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]],
[[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]). Choose reals $M_1, M_2$
witnessing the two conditions at this $\varepsilon$ and let $M$ be the larger of
them, the order being total. Since $A$ is not bounded above there is $x \in A$
with $x > M$, hence with $x > M_1$ and $x > M_2$, and then

$$|L - L'| = |(L - f(x)) + (f(x) - L')| \le |f(x) - L| + |f(x) - L'| < 2\varepsilon = |L - L'|$$

([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-add-order]]),
which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$, and the notation
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x)$ denotes a single real. The same four lines, with the
inequalities on $x$ reversed, give uniqueness at $-\infty$.

**Infinite limits at a point.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We write

$$f(x) \to +\infty \ \text{ as } \ x \to c$$

when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $f(x) > M$ for
every $x \in A$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$; and $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to c$
when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $f(x) < M$ for every
such $x$.

**This library does not write $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = +\infty$.** The right-hand
side would not be an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and writing the equation would
silently move the discussion into the extended real line, a structure that is
not a field. That is the convention already fixed by
[[def-divergence-to-infinity]] for sequences and by [[rem-sup-conventions]] for
suprema, and it is kept here. In particular none of the rules of
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]] may be applied to a function tending to
$\pm\infty$.

**Combined forms.** Let $A$ be not bounded above and $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We
write $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to +\infty$ when for every real $N$ there is a
real $M$ with $f(x) > N$ for every $x \in A$ with $x > M$. The other forms are
obtained the same way, by pairing one of the two conditions on $x$ (unbounded
above, unbounded below) with one of the two conditions on $f(x)$ (above every
real, below every real); each is again a single abbreviation for the displayed
condition, and none of them is an equation.
